user.title: Where are you watching from?
user.description: Passes are predicted on your Home Assistant, from the See A Satellite Tonight catalog of about 900 bright satellites. The location defaults to your home. Two things reveal it: the cloud cover forecast sends its coordinates to Open-Meteo (you can switch this off in the options), and the street view loads map tiles of the surrounding area from OpenFreeMap and AWS.

data_description.name: Used as the device name, for example "Home" or "Cabin".
data_description.location: Where you watch the sky from.
data_description.elevation: Height of the location in metres. A rough value is fine.

reconfigure.title: Move this location
reconfigure.description: Correct where passes are predicted for. The location keeps its entities, and the dashboard cards that show it keep working.

data_description.location: Where you watch the sky from.
data_description.elevation: Height of the location in metres. A rough value is fine.

error.invalid_location: Enter a latitude between -90° and 90° and a valid longitude.
error.cannot_connect: Could not download the satellite catalog. Check that Home Assistant can reach the internet, then try again.
error.unknown: Unexpected error while loading the satellite catalog. The log has the details.

abort.already_configured: This location is already set up.

data.show_in_sidebar: Show Satellite Spotter in the sidebar
data.show_in_calendar: Show the passes in the calendar

data_description.max_magnitude: Only report passes at least this bright. Lower numbers are brighter: 3 is what the website uses, about the faintest you can find from a suburb; 1 keeps the easy ones, and below 0 only the dazzling ones remain.
data_description.cloud_cover: Adds the Open-Meteo cloud cover forecast to each pass. Open-Meteo receives this location's coordinates (to four decimals) every two hours.
data_description.alert_lead_minutes: The "Bright pass soon" sensor turns on this long before a bright pass begins.
data_description.show_in_sidebar: Adds a Satellite Spotter page to the sidebar with the passes, a 3D globe and a street-level view of the sky. The street view loads map tiles of the area around the location from OpenFreeMap and AWS (and from Esri with aerial imagery). The dashboard cards work either way.
data_description.show_in_calendar: Adds a calendar of the passes of the next five days, each with when and where to look. Calendar triggers can then start automations before a pass.
data_description.units: For distances and speeds on the globe and in the street view. "Automatic" follows Home Assistant's unit system.

street_view.name: Street view photos
street_view.description: The street view shows your street in a 360° photo taken near home, or the 3D model where there is none. Panoramax needs no key. Mapillary needs a free access token and Google Street View a Google Cloud API key: with them, those services' photos are offered too. Your browser fetches the photos itself, so it receives the keys.

data_description.street_source: "Best available" takes the best photo near home from every service there is a key for. A single service shows only its photos, and the 3D model none. Each browser can still switch in the street view's Layers menu.
data_description.mapillary_token: Free: on mapillary.com, under Developers, register an application and copy its client token (MLY|…). Mapillary receives the area around home when the street view looks for photos.
data_description.google_api_key: A key of a Google Cloud project with billing on and the Map Tiles API enabled. Restrict it to the Map Tiles API and to your Home Assistant's address. Google's free tier covers about 100,000 tiles a month, and a photo takes about 40 to 140 of them.

error.google_key_needed: Enter a Google Cloud API key to show Google Street View photos.
error.mapillary_token_needed: Enter a Mapillary access token to show Mapillary photos.
error.mapillary_token_format: A Mapillary access token looks like MLY|1234…|abcd…: copy the client token of your application on mapillary.com.

catalog_stale.message: The satellite catalog's orbital elements are {age} days old and could not be refreshed ({error}); predictions are paused until a fresh catalog downloads

catalog_stale_upstream.message: The satellite catalog's orbital elements are {age} days old, and the website's own catalog is just as old; predictions are paused until a fresh catalog downloads

catalog_stale.title: Satellite predictions are paused
catalog_stale.description: The orbital elements in the satellite catalog are {age} days old (the median over all satellites), and no fresher catalog could be downloaded ({error}). Predictions from elements this old would be misleading, so the Satellite Spotter entities are unavailable until a download succeeds. Check that Home Assistant can reach the internet: the catalog comes from the See A Satellite Tonight website. This message goes away by itself once a fresh catalog arrives.

catalog_stale_upstream.title: Satellite predictions are paused
catalog_stale_upstream.description: The orbital elements in the satellite catalog are {age} days old (the median over all satellites), and the See A Satellite Tonight website's own catalog is just as old: there is nothing fresher to download. Predictions from elements this old would be misleading, so the Satellite Spotter entities are unavailable until the website publishes a fresh catalog. There is nothing to fix in Home Assistant: this message goes away by itself once a fresh catalog arrives.
